chapter: Records, Lovie Austin and a first marriage
title: Unissued 1935 American Record Company test sides with Fats Waller
summary: Albertson lists her 1929 Columbia sides and the unissued 1935 titles with Fats Waller on piano; some were risque and test-only, and she was never paid.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Yes. But you made some recordings. Let's see. I'm going to skip to 1929 now. You -- you did for Columbia, you did My Particular Man and Give me All the Love You Got.1)
Well, you're going to skip the other --
the other things that I made before that? You're coming back to it.

No, we're coming back to it, but I wanted to ask you while I remembered this -- in 1935 you did some recordings that were never issued for the American Record Company. And as I recall on one of them there's a piano and guitar accompanying you, and on one of them, you say, play it, Mr. Waller.
That must have been Fats.
And it would seem that way. The titles are 'Drifting Tide', 'You Can't Tell the Difference After Dark', 'Second Hand Man' and 'Send Me a Man'.
Yeah, that was Fats.
Was it Fats, because it sounds like him?
Yes. Yes, that was Fats. I did those for Columbia, huh?
Well, for the American Record Company, which Columbia then later -- or which Columbia bought.
Oh, yes, I see.
And -- but they were never released.
Uh-huh. Those were good songs, but a couple of them were kind of on the suggestive side, I think.
(Simultaneous remarks)
I think Second Hand Man was a little
suggestive.
And 'You Can't Tell the Difference After Dark.'
Yes. Yes, they were a little risqué, and maybe that's why -- but now they'd be knockouts.
Well, they were marked T-O, which means test only. I don't think you ever got paid for doing them.
I didn't.
No.
No. That's --
But you (inaudible).
(Simultaneous remarks)
